title: Install
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Steps checked against the help pages linked under each one on 30 October 2026. Menus change; if what you see differs, tell the maintainer through a GitHub issue.
Installing the plugin gives the assistant instructions only. The plugin itself adds no access to data, to your GitHub account or to anything on your computer; what the assistant app can reach is set in the app.
What you need: a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise), Claude Code, or ChatGPT where Plugin Creator is available. If someone already set the plugin up for your lab, ask them whether you need your own copy.
Pick the assistant you use.

title: Install
section: Claude (on the web, the desktop app or Cowork)
text:
Claude (on the web, the desktop app or Cowork)
You need a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise).
Add the plugin’s marketplace (a marketplace is a list of plugins kept in a GitHub repository):

In Claude, open Settings, then Customize.
Open the Plugins tab.
Click Add, then Add marketplace.



Settings → Customize → Plugins, with the Add menu open.


Choose Add from a repository.
Type VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow and confirm.

If your organization limits which marketplaces you can add, Claude will refuse it; ask your administrator.
Install the plugin:

Still in Customize → Plugins, open the Discover tab.
Select R Analysis Workflow and click Add.

Once installed, it works in chat on the web, the Chat tab of the desktop app, Cowork, and Claude Code when you sign in with the same account.
Source: Anthropic, Use plugins in Claude. Tried by the maintainer in Cowork with version 0.1.14 on 3 November 2026 (see VALIDATION.md).

title: Install
text:
Claude Code
You need Claude Code version 2.1.292 or later for the one-line install.
Install, in your terminal (not inside a Claude Code session):
claude plugin install r-analysis-workflow --marketplace VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow
It should print that it added the marketplace and then installed the plugin. To check, run claude plugin list: you should see r-analysis-workflow@r-analysis-workflow. The plugin loads the next time you start Claude Code.
On an older version, use two commands instead:
claude plugin marketplace add VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow
claude plugin install r-analysis-workflow@r-analysis-workflow
Updates. Claude Code does not update plugins from this marketplace automatically unless you turn it on. Either:

turn it on once: inside a Claude Code session type /plugin, go to the Marketplaces tab, select r-analysis-workflow, then select Enable auto-update; or
update by hand when you want to, in your terminal:

claude plugin update r-analysis-workflow@r-analysis-workflow
Installing in Claude Code puts the plugin in Claude Code only. To use it in Claude chat or Cowork, add it there too, as in the Claude section above; a plugin added there also reaches Claude Code.
Sources: Claude Code docs, Install and manage plugins and Plugin commands reference. The install from GitHub was tested in a sandbox with Claude Code 2.1.314 (VALIDATION.md).

title: Install
text:
ChatGPT
In ChatGPT you make the plugin with OpenAI’s Plugin Creator, pointing it at this repository. Whether Plugin Creator is available depends on your plan and workspace; OpenAI’s help pages don’t list the plans.
Create the plugin:

Start a new conversation.
Type @, search for Plugin Creator, and select it.
Ask it, in your own words: Create a plugin from the plugin/ folder of https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow.
Answer its questions and follow its prompts to finish. Check that the name is R Analysis Workflow.

Use it: in a new conversation, type @, start typing “R Analysis Workflow”, and select it under Plugins.
Update it when a new version comes out:

Open Plugins and select R Analysis Workflow.
Choose Edit Plugin.
Ask it to update the plugin from the plugin/ folder of the same repository, keeping its name.

Sources: OpenAI, Build plugins (steps 1, 2 and 4, using it, and updating) and Plugins in ChatGPT.
What has and hasn’t been checked:

OpenAI’s pages describe Plugin Creator building a plugin from your description and files. They don’t describe creating one from a GitHub repository (step 3). The maintainer tried step 3 with this layout on 30 October 2026 and it worked.
Updating through Edit Plugin from the repository has not been tried with this plugin.
Uploading a ZIP of the plugin/ folder: OpenAI’s help page mentions uploading a plugin but gives no steps, and it has not been tried with this layout. GitHub’s Download ZIP button gives the whole repository, not the plugin/ folder, so it is not the right file.
Workspace administrators can import plugins from a GitHub marketplace that syncs daily, but this repository does not have the catalog file ChatGPT needs for that.

title: Problems it solves
text:
Written for version 0.1.14.
Each entry names a problem an analysis project can run into, the plugin rule that addresses it, the version that added the rule, and how it fared in testing. Entries are ordered by the stage of a project where the problem arises.
What this page does and doesn’t claim. It describes risks the plugin is built to handle. It does not claim what would happen without the plugin: no run has yet compared the same scenario with and without it. The test results come from simulated users (see How it’s tested). Versions before 0.1.7 are not recorded in this repository, so rules from then are marked “before 0.1.7”.
Test results use the scorecards’ scale: ✔ worked as intended, ~ worked partly or only because a person caught it, ✘ failed, not yet tested.

title: Problems it solves
text:
Getting the plugin to work

The assistant can’t open the plugin’s shared guidance

The risk: ChatGPT’s skills package only each skill’s own folder, so guidance shared between skills was out of reach and every skill ran without it.
What the plugin does: keeps one source copy of each shared file and generates a copy inside every skill that uses it (build_skills.py); the release check fails if a copy is stale.
Since: 0.1.10.
Tested: each skill folder resolves every link inside itself when copied alone; not yet tested in ChatGPT (VALIDATION.md).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Starting a project

A novice can’t get from an idea to a working repository

The risk: someone with no GitHub account and no R is asked to install tools, learn Git and set up a repository before anything useful happens.
What the plugin does: a short questionnaire, one question at a time, reusing what is already known, with no installs until the work needs them (initialize-analysis).
Since: before 0.1.7; setting up from R added in 0.1.12.
Tested: ✔ a novice went from nothing to a public repository, protected main branch, setup notes, a draft pull request and her own assistant project in one session (0.1.8 scorecard).



The main branch is unprotected, or the website never goes live

The risk: a repository’s rules say changes go through pull requests when nothing enforces it, or a site is built but never switched on.
What the plugin does: gives the maintainer the steps to protect the default branch and switch on GitHub Pages, reminds them when the first site is merged, and offers a check that reads the actual settings rather than assuming them (GitHub workflow).
Since: Pages reminder 0.1.7; the settings check 0.1.12.
Tested: not yet tested. The 0.1.12 check has not been run (VALIDATION.md).



Data or secrets end up in a public repository

The risk: data files, credentials or outputs not yet cleared are committed, and deleting them later doesn’t remove them from history.
What the plugin does: a .gitignore adapted to the project and reviewed before the first commit, the full file list read before committing, and steps for what to do if something was pushed by mistake (data handling).
Since: .gitignore before 0.1.7; reading the file list and the steps after a mistake 0.1.12.
Tested: the ignore rules were tested with git check-ignore in a scratch repository (VALIDATION.md).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Deciding the science

Someone settles a scientific question who shouldn’t

The risk: someone on the project, or an assistant, quietly chooses a cut-off, covariate or exclusion in code, and nobody can later say who decided or why.
What the plugin does: the analysis plan decides; every open choice is a decision issue on GitHub settled only by a named decider; assistants draft options and never choose (analysis plan). The deciders are asked for at setup.
Since: before 0.1.7; deciders asked at setup 0.1.8.
Tested: ✔ across two student leads, an impatient statistician and a clinician who used only email (0.1.8 scorecard); ✔ through peer review six months later (continuation scorecard).



Input from a collaborator who doesn’t use GitHub is lost

The risk: a clinician’s decision arrives by email or in a meeting, lives in one person’s inbox, and is gone when they leave.
What the plugin does: whoever received it posts the decider’s exact words in the decision issue, with name, date and how it was given; a summary from memory doesn’t settle anything (analysis plan).
Since: 0.1.8.
Tested: ✔ throughout (0.1.8 scorecard). ✘ on consent: a collaborator’s whole email was posted to a public repository before she knew it was public; no rule yet covers this.



A decision is credited to the wrong person

The risk: a draft says “Dr. X decided” when Dr. X didn’t, or puts someone’s words in another’s mouth.
What the plugin does: writing that a person decided, said or wrote something needs a link to the record; if there is none, the assistant asks instead (conventions).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ~ in 0.1.8, before the rule, two wrong attributions were caught only by the people concerned (continuation scorecard); ✔ in the 0.1.9 re-test, where an agreement given only verbally was not asserted (0.1.9 scorecard).



The plan changes after results are seen, without a record

The risk: a locked plan is edited once results are in, and a reader can’t tell what was planned from what was chosen afterwards.
What the plugin does: at locking, an empty “Amendments after locking” section and a tag; every later change gets a dated entry saying whether it was made before or after outcome data were seen, and a new tag (analysis plan).
Since: the amendment rule before 0.1.9; the empty section at locking 0.1.9.
Tested: ~ in 0.1.8 the rule never reached the repository and three claims about when results had been seen proved false (continuation scorecard); ✔ in the 0.1.9 re-test, the section was added at locking (0.1.9 scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Working with an assistant

Something is posted in a person’s name that they never saw

The risk: an assistant posts an issue comment, a pull-request description or an email as the person, with wording they wouldn’t have used.
What the plugin does: shows the exact text first and waits for a go-ahead, unless the person’s own instructions waive it (conventions).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ mostly held, with two conflicts with other rules (0.1.8 scorecard); ✔ throughout the continuation, where it let a person correct the provenance of his own text before it was posted (continuation scorecard).



Work is left in a chat or a download, and lost

The risk: a new chat remembers nothing, so a draft that lives only in an old chat or a downloads folder is gone.
What the plugin does: at the end of a session, asks whether anything unfinished should be saved to the repository and offers where (conventions); a check-in looks for drafts that never got there (onboarding).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ worked in most sessions; failed once, when prepared changes were kept as downloads and one was lost (0.1.8 scorecard).



The assistant asks too much, or too little

The risk: a novice is swamped by questions, or an assistant builds a whole setup on its own reading of the first request.
What the plugin does: how much to ask depends on the working style the person chose (review only, step by step, or hands-off), step by step when none is set, with rules that hold in every style (conventions).
Since: working styles 0.1.7; one consolidated rule 0.1.11.
Tested: not yet tested in a simulated session under each style (VALIDATION.md).



Directions to click through menus that don’t exist

The risk: an assistant describes a menu path from memory, and a novice can’t find it.
What the plugin does: use the plugin’s own steps, check the app’s current help pages, or say it isn’t sure and describe what to look for (conventions).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ in the 0.1.9 re-test, one click path for GitHub was given with no source and not flagged as unchecked (0.1.9 scorecard).



Code written from memory for the wrong package version

The risk: code works against the version the assistant remembers, not the one installed, and fails or silently changes results.
What the plugin does: read the documentation of the installed version, including its news; test past any fake once against the real package; name the version relied on in the pull request (AGENTS.md template).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ✔ read the project’s locked version and its documentation, and said plainly what it couldn’t run; ✘ the suggested pull-request text didn’t name the version (0.1.9 scorecard).



Code a clinician-analyst can’t read

The risk: assistant-written R is dense with constructs that someone who learned R from online guides can’t follow, so nobody on the team can check it.
What the plugin does: a readable-R rule for new code, and any style-only change to tested code must show identical outputs (conventions).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ✔ on new code early in the continuation; not yet on a large new analysis (continuation scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Code and the website

The website stops describing the actual code

The risk: a page holds a pasted copy of code that has since changed, so readers are told the analysis does something it doesn’t.
What the plugin does: pages import labelled sections from the scripts themselves, and are updated in the same pull request as the code (document-analysis).
Since: before 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ pages imported the real code; ~ pages went stale between pull requests (0.1.8 scorecard).



Readers can’t tell what is still undecided

The risk: a page describes a method as if it were settled when the decision is still open, and a reader quotes it.
What the plugin does: any text that depends on an open decision is highlighted in yellow, linked to its decision issue, with a note at the top of the page (Quarto guidance).
Since: 0.1.14.
Tested: not yet tested in a user simulation; the marks were checked in a rendered starter (VALIDATION.md).



Pull requests pile up and nobody knows the merge order

The risk: a change built on another unmerged change leaves the reviewer to work out an order, and conflicts follow.
What the plugin does: every pull request is based on the default branch; a change that needs an unmerged one waits for it or is folded into it (GitHub workflow).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ test merges before advising; a stacked branch kept off a pull request until its base merged (0.1.8 scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Review

A review misses part of what changed

The risk: a reviewer reads the file the author mentioned and misses an unrelated file that came along in the same commit.
What the plugin does: a change review reads every file the change touches and lists them; a file not read is named, with the reason (review-analysis).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ✔ in the 0.1.9 re-test, all four planted defects across five files were found, plus one that wasn’t planted (0.1.9 scorecard).



A reviewer’s claimed error isn’t real

The risk: an assistant reviewer reports a confident error that doesn’t hold, and someone acts on it.
What the plugin does: five blind reviewers, and a combining step that checks every claimed error against the source before listing it (reviewers).
Since: before 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ in the blind review at the end of the 0.1.8 simulation, each reviewer stayed in role, unverifiable claims were marked as such, and no data rule was breached (0.1.8 scorecard). ✘ the full panel was never offered for the pull request that implemented the primary analysis.

title: Problems it solves
text:
Going public

Results go public before anyone meant them to

The risk: tables, figures or estimates reach a public repository or website before they are cleared, or before the paper.
What the plugin does: whether outputs are tracked is decided at setup and the reason recorded; no results in code, comments or other repository text; a Release review before anything goes public, then a person signs off (data handling, review-analysis).
Since: 0.1.8 to 0.1.12 (results out of repository text 0.1.8; the reason for ignoring outputs 0.1.9; the Disclosure check 0.1.12).
Tested: ~ in the continuation, outputs tracked by the project’s .gitignore would have carried real estimates to the public repository while the assistant advised keeping them off, and its own audit of what was public was incomplete (continuation scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Handing over

The next lead can’t find out where things stand

The risk: the lead leaves, and the next one has only a repository link and no idea what was done, decided or promised.
What the plugin does: the next person starts from the repository, not the last person’s files; leaving follows four steps (documents, open work, pending requests, ownership), started by the person or by a check-in that sees their end date (onboarding).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ the hand-over was started by the plugin’s own scheduled reminder, and the next lead rebuilt the state from the repository in one reply (0.1.8 scorecard).



Transferring the repository breaks the website

The risk: the person who owns the repository leaves; after the transfer the old site address stops working, because GitHub doesn’t redirect websites.
What the plugin does: raises the transfer before the owner leaves, orders it last, and lists the links to update and the site to switch on again (onboarding).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ the transfer was done in the right order, but old links were still on the site at the end (0.1.8 scorecard).

title: How it’s tested
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Full procedure: testing/README.md.
A plugin is a set of instructions, so testing it means watching assistants follow those instructions and checking what they actually did. Two tests do this, both run by an orchestrating agent that starts independent assistants, passes messages between them and keeps the record. Neither needs ChatGPT itself. They stand in for real use, which remains the final check.

title: How it’s tested
text:
How a run is recorded

Before a run, its starting point is written down: the plugin commit, and for a run that doesn’t start from nothing, the simulated world it starts from and every defect planted in it, with what passing looks like. These are the setups.
During a run, every gap is logged as it appears: something the plugin didn’t cover, something it made go right, or a tension between two of its rules.
After a run, the repository keeps its scorecard and run notes (environment, setup used, and anything the orchestrator got wrong). Transcripts and the gap log are working material and are kept outside the repository. Each gap still open becomes an issue on the plugin’s repository.
Then the plugin is fixed from those issues, one decision at a time by the maintainer, and the affected part is run again.

The list of runs is on Runs. What the fixes add up to is on Problems it solves.

title: How it’s tested
text:
What the tests can’t show

How ChatGPT or Claude themselves behave with the plugin installed. The assistants in the tests follow the plugin as written, in a sandbox.
What happens with real restricted data. Tests use public or made-up data only.
What happens without the plugin. No run has yet compared the same scenario without it.

title: Runs
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Records: testing/runs. Every person named in them is a simulated persona.
One line per run, newest first. Each record has a scorecard (what worked, what partly worked, what failed, with the evidence) and run notes (setup, environment, and anything the orchestrator got wrong).

title: Protecting main and Pages
text: Written for version 0.1.14. Part of On GitHub, not in files, which lists the sources.

title: Protecting main and Pages
Protecting main and Pages
text:
GitHub Pages
What it is. The GitHub feature that puts the project website online. The website is built from the repository, but it goes live only after GitHub Pages is turned on.
Who turns it on. Someone with admin or maintainer permission on the repository. When a project is set up, the assistant reminds the person setting up that this step is needed, or the site will not appear. Agents cannot change the setting; they tell the person who can.
When, for each publishing route. During setup the project chooses how the site is published, and AGENTS.md records the choice.








Publishing route
When to turn on Pages
What to choose




The rendered site (the docs/ folder) is committed to the repository. This is the default.
Once the first pull request containing docs/ has been merged
The default branch and the /docs folder


A GitHub Actions workflow builds and publishes the site, and docs/ is not committed
Once the workflow has run on the default branch and created the gh-pages branch
The gh-pages branch and the / (root) folder



On the website, both routes start at Settings, then Pages, then Source: Deploy from a branch. A maintainer working in R can turn on Pages for the docs/ route with one usethis command that the plugin gives. The workflow route needs a publish workflow file, which the plugin does not yet provide.
A limit. As with branch protection, a private repository on the free GitHub plan has no GitHub Pages.

title: Issues, pull requests and milestones
text: Written for version 0.1.14. Part of On GitHub, not in files, which lists the sources.

title: Issues, pull requests and milestones
text:
Issues
What they are. GitHub issues hold three kinds of open item:

Decision issues: one open scientific question each, settled only by a named decider (see The plan and its decisions).
Gaps between code and plan: places where the code does not yet do what the plan says.
Known defects: things that are wrong.

Labels and templates. Each project chooses its own labels, templates and conventions. The plugin prescribes none.
What the assistant does with them. It drafts a decision issue for each choice the plan leaves open, rather than choosing. Before asking anyone a question, it looks in the issues (and the plan, AGENTS.md and pull requests) for the answer. Before posting a comment as a person, it shows them the exact text and waits for their go-ahead, unless their own instructions say otherwise.
For someone joining or taking over. The open issues, with the plan and the open pull requests, are where a newcomer finds the project’s state. The assistant starts there, not from the previous person’s files or chats.

title: Issues, pull requests and milestones
text:
Pull requests
What they are. A pull request offers a set of changes, made on a separate branch, for merging into the main branch. Any tool that creates a branch and opens a pull request will do; each person uses what they prefer, and the plugin does not prescribe one.
The rules. Good practice for everyone, and required of agents:

One branch per piece of work, not one per commit.
Based on the main branch. If a change needs another that has not been merged yet, wait for that one to merge, or fold both into one pull request. Pull requests are not stacked on each other, so no one is left to work out an order to merge them in.
The website follows the change. When docs/ is committed, the site is re-rendered on the same branch as the change it reflects.
It says what it addresses and what was checked. Each pull request names the plan section or issue it addresses. It says what was checked, from the list in the project’s AGENTS.md (for example: does the change follow the plan and leave every open decision open; does it avoid any number that could come from restricted data). A pull request opened by an agent also says whether the checks were done by running code on synthetic data or by reading only, and never calls synthetic results “results”.
Closing a decision issue. A pull request that settles a decision issue includes the plan change and the line Closes #<n>, where <n> is the issue’s number. GitHub then closes the issue when the pull request is merged.

Who merges. A person. An agent may commit to a branch and open a pull request, but never merges one.

title: Issues, pull requests and milestones
text:
Milestones (optional)
What they are. A milestone groups issues and pull requests under one phase of the project, with a target date, so anyone can see what that phase is waiting on. A decision issue placed in a milestone shows which phase it holds up. GitHub’s Milestones page shows each milestone’s due date and how many of its items are closed.
Who chooses. Milestones are optional. During setup the assistant asks whether the project wants them. If so, the team gives the phases and dates; for example, plan locked, cohort built, models fitted, manuscript drafted.
What the assistant does. If its GitHub connection can create milestones and assign items, it may do this once the person has given the phases and dates. Otherwise it walks them through the steps on the GitHub website.

title: The setup note and check-ins
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Part of On GitHub, not in files, which lists the sources.
The setup note. Setting up a project asks one question at a time, and can stretch over several sessions. The assistant records the setup decisions made so far, and the questions still open, in one place the project agrees on: a setup note, or a tracker the project already uses. Nothing sensitive goes there, and no one’s personal permissions. A later session resumes from this record instead of asking everything again.
Saving unfinished work. At the end of a working session, the assistant asks whether anything unfinished should be saved to the repository: a draft pull request, an issue comment marked as a draft, or a new issue. A new chat will not remember it. Anything holding results from restricted data that are not cleared for release stays where it is, and the person is told why.
Check-ins (optional). Anyone, whatever their role, can ask for a periodic check-in, using the assistant’s scheduled tasks where the assistant has them. The person chooses how often it runs. It always reports what is waiting on them:

issues assigned to them;
decisions they make, each with the question, each option in a line, and a link to the decision issue. They can decide from the check-in or open the issue, but the decision itself is recorded in the issue;
pull requests awaiting their review.

They can also choose to include what they are waiting on from others, work with no recent activity, and milestones due soon. The check-in can look over their recent chats for drafts that never reached the repository, and, if they have email connected and want it, their project email, proposing where to record each decision or request it finds. It reads the repository; it may draft messages but never sends or posts anything on its own. The person’s check-in choices are kept in their own instructions, not in the project’s shared files.
Leaving a project. When someone leaves or hands over work, the assistant goes through it with them before their last session: moving anything that exists only in a chat, on a laptop or in email into the repository (subject to the project’s disclosure rules); deciding for each open issue and pull request whether to finish it, hand it on, close it with a reason, or mark it paused with what it is waiting on; and recording requests to others that have no answer yet. Not everything can be finished or given an owner, and a project may go dormant; the assistant records what stays open and why.
Transferring ownership. If the person leaving owns the repository, the assistant raises transferring it to the PI. The plugin’s steps are Settings → General → Transfer, and the new owner must accept within a day. Issues, pull requests and history move with the repository, and old links to the repository redirect to the new one.
The website caveat. GitHub does not redirect the website. After a transfer, someone must update the site and repository links in _quarto.yml, the site pages and the README, re-render the site, and turn GitHub Pages on again under the new owner.

title: Blueprint and personal instructions
text: Written for version 0.1.14. Part of Rules for working, which lists the sources.

title: Blueprint and personal instructions
text:
REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md
What it is. The intended layout of an R analysis repository: which folders and files exist and what each is for. ARCHITECTURE.md describes what the project has actually built; the blueprint describes what it aims for.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository. It must be there before the website is first rendered, and the site shows it on its own page.
What’s in it. A tree of the layout, with a one-line note on each part: the R/ folder with main.R, setup.R, functions.R, tables.R and figures.R; figures/ and tables/; references/ for supporting literature; quarto/ for the website pages; docs/ for the rendered site; and the root files (analysis-plan.md, references.bib, AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, the README and .gitignore). Some files are marked optional, such as a licence or an RStudio project file. Short notes follow on scripts, documentation and which outputs to keep in Git.
Who edits it. It is kept unchanged. The assistant copies the plugin’s blueprint into the project as it is. What the project has actually built goes in ARCHITECTURE.md instead.

title: Blueprint and personal instructions
text:
Personal project instructions
What they are. Each person’s own instructions for their AI assistant, kept in their own assistant project for this repository (the plugin calls it an “LLM project”). They tell the assistant who you are, how much help you want, and what it may do for you, so each chat starts with that context instead of you pasting it again.
Where they live. Outside the repository, in your own assistant project, one project per repository. They are not shared. The repository stays the shared record: nothing others need should live only in your project.
What’s in them. The plugin’s template asks for:

the project, its repository and default branch, and how you work with GitHub (through the assistant, from your own tools, or both);
your role and the help you want, for example guided learning, review, or working together on code;
your working style, chosen from three starting points and adjusted to suit you:








Style
What the assistant does




Review only
Reads, reviews and suggests; changes nothing


Step by step
Proposes each change, waits for your yes, then makes it on a branch and explains it


Hands-off
Builds on branches and opens pull requests without asking at each step, then walks you through what it made




which actions it is authorized to take, kept separate (editing, running code, installing, commits and pull requests, comments, publishing);
your data boundaries, by pointing to approved locations and agreements, never with credentials;
whether it may post anything as you without showing you first (by default it shows you the exact text);
whether you want a periodic check-in and what it should report.

In every style, nothing else is posted or sent as you without your approval, another way of writing something already agreed is shown to you before it is committed, and scientific decisions stay with the deciders. Hands-off covers only the pull requests it opens.
What they never hold. Copies of the analysis plan, the blueprint or the shared review steps. They can be stricter than AGENTS.md, and then the assistant follows them. They never loosen its rules on data, decisions or pull requests.
Who edits them. You. One person’s working style or permissions are never carried into someone else’s instructions or into the shared files.
What the assistant does with them. When someone sets up or joins a project, the assistant offers to fill in the template, asking which working style they want and how they work with GitHub. It is an offer, not a requirement. If it cannot change your assistant’s settings itself, it gives you the text to paste and says so.

title: .gitignore
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Part of Rules for working, which lists the sources.
What it is. A list of files and folders that Git should leave out, so they are never added to the repository by accident.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository. Some apps hide files whose names start with a dot, so the plugin also keeps a visible copy of its template.
What’s in it. The assistant adapts the plugin’s starter template to each project rather than copying it blindly. The template has groups for:

R and editor files (saved sessions, history, settings);
Quarto’s working files;
credentials such as .Renviron and key files;
common data formats (.csv, .rds, .sas7bdat, .parquet and others) and a data-raw/ folder, as a safety net, since data should live outside the repository anyway;
figures/ and tables/, when they need review before release;
narrow exceptions for approved files, for example !tests/fixtures/synthetic.csv. Exceptions are kept narrow and never cover a whole format.

How figures/, tables/ and docs/ are decided. At setup, two questions decide them.








Question at setup
Answer
Effect




Do the figures and tables need review before they can be public?
Yes
figures/ and tables/ stay ignored until the named review clears them; AGENTS.md names the review



No
They are tracked from the start


How is the website published?
From the committed docs/ folder
docs/ is tracked



By a GitHub Actions workflow
docs/ is ignored; the workflow publishes the same pages



The assistant asks the first question directly rather than guessing from the data sources. When a review later clears the outputs, someone removes the two lines and inspects the contents before adding them. Tables saved as .csv or .rds stay hidden by the data-format lines even then, so cleared tables need their own exceptions.
What it never does. Ignoring a file doesn’t remove it from history: anything already committed stays in Git’s history, in forks and in everyone’s copies. It doesn’t control access either: an ignored folder inside the project is still readable by any AI tool connected to that folder. That is why the plugin prefers keeping restricted data in a separate folder outside the project. File names can’t identify every sensitive file; text, images, logs and other outputs can hold restricted information too.
If something was pushed by mistake. Stop pushing. Revoke any password, token or key first. For restricted data, tell the PI and whoever the agreement names; the agreement decides what follows. Removing it from history is the maintainer’s job, following GitHub’s guide on removing sensitive data. Agents do not attempt it.
What the assistant does with it. It adapts the template, checks that the rules cover the project’s real output folders without hiding source files, and reports any tracked file that looks sensitive without opening it. It can confirm a rule works with git check-ignore --no-index -v. It doesn’t untrack, delete or rewrite history unless someone with the authority to do so asks.

title: AGENTS.md
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Part of Rules for working, which lists the sources.
What it is. The rules for working in the repository, for everyone: the people on the project and any AI agents working for them. It covers conventions, data handling and checks. It opens by dividing the documentation into four places, each covering its own topic without repeating the others:







Where
Covers




analysis-plan.md
What the analysis is meant to do


ARCHITECTURE.md
How the code is built: scripts, data flow, and the objects passed between them


AGENTS.md
How to work in the repository: rules, conventions and checks


GitHub Issues
Open scientific decisions (decision issues), gaps between code and plan, and known defects



Where it lives. At the top of the repository. The project website shows it on a page that only includes the root file, so you edit the root file, never the page.
What’s in it. The plugin’s template has these sections. Parts in angle brackets are filled in for each project.

The project. One paragraph on the question and the data. Then the standing rules: the analysis plan is the source of truth, and code that needs to depart from it goes to a decision issue first. The deciders are named here with their areas; anyone may add to a decision issue, but only a decider settles it. It also says this is an analysis, not an R package, and names the default branch (the main version of the project). That branch is protected: changes reach it only through pull requests (proposed changes that others can review before they are merged).
Data sources and what agents may do. A table with one row per data source the analysis uses: the source, the package that loads it, the package’s documentation, whether the team maintains that package or it is external, how access is restricted, and what AI agents may do with it. Code that touches a source goes through its package. For a restricted source, the agents’ column starts at “None: code, documentation and synthetic data only”. Only a person can widen it, through a pull request that names the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose this change, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it. The template then splits the rules: problems in a package the team maintains are fixed or reported in that package; problems in an external package are worked around in the project’s own code, and whether to report them upstream is the person’s call.
Exploration and definitive analysis. Exploring on a branch or fork is welcome, and its findings are labelled preliminary. A script joins the definitive analysis when R/main.R runs it; from then on every rule applies.
Scripts and labels. R/main.R runs everything in order. Each script does one job and starts with a short header saying what it needs and what it makes. Settings a reader might want to change (a window, a year, a threshold) are named once in R/setup.R. Scripts are divided into labelled sections, marked with a comment line like ## ---- compute-summary, so the website can show the real code. Labels are unique across all scripts, because a repeated label silently shows the wrong code. Analysis variables carry readable labels, with units and time windows. No script, comment, commit message, issue or pull request contains results from restricted data unless they are cleared for release.
Website. The site explains the code and never runs the analysis. It lists the page layout, the colour and icon for each kind of page, and the yellow highlight for content an open decision could change. It records the project’s publishing route: either the rendered docs/ folder is committed and served by GitHub Pages, or a GitHub Actions workflow renders and publishes the site. A new definitive script gets its page in the same pull request.
Outputs. Tables and figures are written to tables/ and figures/. The project states whether they are tracked or kept out of Git until a named review clears them, and if they are kept out, whether that is because of restricted data or only publication timing. Published figures need alt text.
Restricted data. These rules apply to everyone. Data and anything derived from patient-level records are never committed. AI agents never open restricted data, or outputs from it that are not yet cleared; anything an agent opens is sent to the model provider. Agents write and test code on synthetic data: made-up data built in code and labelled as such. Real results come from an authorized person. The section also holds the agreement’s small-cell rule and the rules for keys, tokens and paid services.
Coding conventions. The participant flow (the cohort and its STROBE diagram) comes from one piece of code using the flowchart package. Code lists are checked against the official code sets, and joins are checked so rows don’t multiply. Package functions are checked against their documentation rather than written from memory. The style is meant to be readable by a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides.
Checks for any change. A checklist to run before opening a pull request: does the change follow the plan and leave open decisions open; are the cohort counts reproducible; is ARCHITECTURE.md current; does any site page run analysis code; could anything changed reveal restricted data; does main.R run in a fresh session? A project adds checks its own design needs.
Working with agents. Each person sets their agent’s working style in their own instructions; without one, the agent works step by step. At most, an agent edits code and documents, runs code and renders the site on synthetic data, commits to a branch and opens a pull request. Under any style, an agent never merges a pull request, never chooses among the options in a decision issue, asks before running the full pipeline or expensive calls, and shows a person the exact text before posting anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions say otherwise.

Who edits it. Anyone, through a pull request. Widening what agents may do with a restricted source is a person’s change, made as described above.
What the assistant does with it. It reads AGENTS.md, the plan and ARCHITECTURE.md before making changes. During setup it adapts the template to the project. It fills the data sources table from the code that actually loads the data, not from memory, and asks about any source whose package or access terms are unclear. It asks who the deciders are, and if materials such as an IRB protocol name investigators, suggests them for the person to confirm. If no one is named yet, the line stays marked as still to fill, and decision issues can be drafted but not settled.

title: The code
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Source: starter scripts, AGENTS.md template, shared conventions, repository blueprint, document-analysis skill, data sources, reporting.
The analysis itself is a set of R scripts in the repository’s R/ folder. This page explains what each standard script is for, how a script is laid out so the website can show it, the difference between exploring and the definitive analysis, and ARCHITECTURE.md, the file that describes the code as it is actually built. Two rules apply to every script: the R must be readable, and code that touches a data source goes through that source’s package.

title: The code
text:
R/main.R
What it is. The one script that runs the whole definitive analysis. It does no analysis of its own; it runs (“sources”) the other scripts one after another, in the order each needs the one before. A typical order is setup, then building the cohort, then processing, then modelling, then the outputs.
Where it lives. R/main.R. It is run from the project’s top folder, in a fresh R session, using only relative paths.
What’s in it. A short list of source() lines. The starter version looks like this:
source("R/setup.R")
source("R/functions.R")
source("R/example.R")
# source("R/tables.R")
# source("R/figures.R")
Who edits it. Whoever adds a definitive script puts its source() line at the right point, in the same pull request that adds the script.
What the assistant does with it. It reads main.R to learn which scripts are definitive and in what order. It asks before running the full pipeline. On restricted data, results are produced by an authorised person, not by the assistant.

title: The code
The code
text:
R/functions.R
What it is. The home for reusable helper functions: steps the analysis does more than once, or steps worth checking on their own. A large project may split them into subfolders instead.
What’s in it. Named functions. Each takes everything it needs as arguments and doesn’t reach for objects defined elsewhere, so it can be tested on its own. Some functions must be tested on synthetic data (made-up data built in code) with a known answer:

code that turns model output into reported numbers;
any step that needs base R (for example matrix algebra for pooling), kept inside a named function with a comment saying why.

It also holds wrappers: when an external package’s function has a problem, the project wraps it here, with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue.

title: The code
section: A definitive script and its labelled sections
text:
A definitive script and its labelled sections
What it is. A script that does one job in the analysis, such as building the cohort or fitting a model, and is sourced from main.R. The starter’s R/example.R is a synthetic example of one.
The header comment. Each script starts with a few comment lines saying what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces:
# Purpose: synthetic demonstration of a definitive analysis step.
# Needs: demonstration_multiplier (setup.R), scale_values() (functions.R).
# Produces: demonstration_summary. Uses no data and writes no files.
Labelled sections. The script is divided into sections, each starting with a label line such as ## ---- compute-summary. A label covers the code from its line down to the next label. Labels:

mark every logical step;
are lower-case words joined by hyphens, describing the step;
are unique across all scripts, because a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code;
are comments, so they never change what the code does.

The labels exist for the website. Each script’s page imports the script and shows each labelled section next to prose explaining it, so the site shows the actual code rather than a copy that can go stale. Before renaming or deleting a label, search the website pages for it.
Exploratory and definitive scripts. Exploring is welcome on a branch or a fork. An exploratory script doesn’t need to be sourced from main.R or have a website page, and anything it finds is labelled preliminary. A script becomes definitive when main.R sources it. From then on every rule on this page applies, and the same pull request also:

labels the script and gives it its header comment;
adds its website page and sidebar entry;
updates ARCHITECTURE.md.

What it never holds. Results, counts or data values from restricted data that aren’t cleared for release, whether in the code, its comments or its commit messages. That holds for exploratory scripts too.

title: The code
text:
R/tables.R and R/figures.R
What they are. The scripts that make the outputs. Each can build its outputs directly or run more specialised scripts that do. In the starter main.R their lines are commented out until the project has outputs to make.
What they produce. Tables saved to tables/ and figures saved to figures/, following the reporting guidance:







Output
Built with




Participant flow (STROBE) diagram
flowchart, from the same code that builds the cohort


Descriptions, Table 1, model tables
gtsummary


Figures
ggplot2, following the PSI graphics principles, each with a caption and alt text


Survival curves
ggsurvfit, KMunicate style: confidence intervals and a table of numbers at risk, censored and with events



What it never holds. Counts below the governing small-cell rule. Flowchart boxes and risk tables are checked against it before they leave the approved environment.
Tracked or not. Whether tables/ and figures/ are committed to the repository is the project’s choice, recorded in its AGENTS.md. Outputs from restricted data stay out of the repository until the governing review clears them.

title: The code
text:
ARCHITECTURE.md
What it is. A description of the code as it is actually built: the scripts, how data flows between them, and the objects they pass along. It complements two other files. REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md is the intended layout, kept unchanged from the plugin; analysis-plan.md is what the analysis must do.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository. The project website shows it on its Architecture page, read from this one file.
What’s in it. Only what is implemented now. It names the commit it describes and says whether uncommitted changes were included.
What it never holds. Planned work or how far the work has got. Those belong in the plan and in GitHub issues.
Who edits it. Whoever makes a structural change: a script added, removed or reordered, or a change in how data flows between scripts. It is refreshed in the same pull request.
What the assistant does with it. It refreshes the file after such a change, using Posit’s describe-design skill if that is installed, and says so if it isn’t.

title: The code
The code
text:
Data sources and their packages
Each source the analysis loads is listed in the project’s AGENTS.md with the package that reads it, and code that touches a source goes through that package. Scripts don’t rewrite loading, cleaning or definitions that the package already provides. The table also says whether each package is maintained by the project’s team or is external:

Team package: problems are fixed in the package, or wrapped in the project with a comment linking the package’s issue until it is fixed.
External package: problems are worked around in R/functions.R, with a comment explaining why.
No package: one loading script records where the data came from, which release, and any processing.

The same table says what AI agents may do with each source. For a restricted source the answer starts as “None: code, documentation and synthetic data only”.

title: The pages in quarto/
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Part of The website, which lists the sources.
Each kind of page has one sidebar icon and one colour. A page that doesn’t fit takes the kind of its main content; for example, a page of historical code is R code. The kind is only a label: it doesn’t make anything publishable.

Clinical background (background.qmd) gives the clinical or scientific reason for the question, with citations from references.bib.
Methodological background (methodological_background.qmd) explains, in general terms and without code, the knowledge the methods rest on: what the data sources are, how records become an outcome, how comparison groups are chosen, why the models fit. It holds nothing specific to this study: no study numbers, and no links to the plan or to issues.
Study design and methods (study_methods.qmd) explains in plain language what this study chose and why. Each section carries up to three kinds of note:

Specified in: the section of the analysis plan that defines the method, linked.
Current code: where the code doesn’t yet do what the plan says, what it does now, with a link to the GitHub issue tracking the gap.
Decision pending: a choice the plan hasn’t made yet, linked to its decision issue. These are highlighted in yellow.

It starts as one page. When it grows, it is split into a section of pages chosen for the study, each opening with a line that points back to the key to the notes, and study_methods.qmd stays the first page so links to it keep working.
One page per script. Each script that R/main.R runs gets its own page, named after it: R/create_cohort.R gets quarto/create_cohort.qmd. The pages sit under Code, in three groups: Setup and helper functions, Data processing and analysis, and Tables and figures (once those scripts exist). A page has:

A one-sentence purpose.
A pink Rcode box linking the script on GitHub and the helper scripts it depends on.
A hidden chunk that reads the script’s code: knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R").
One section per labelled step of the script. Each has prose, then an empty chunk that shows that step’s code without running it.

The labels are comment lines in the script, such as ## ---- compute-summary. Because the page pulls in the actual script, the code you read on the site is the code that runs; there is no second copy to drift. The prose explains purpose, inputs, the change made, the assumptions and plan sections behind it, and what the step hands on to later scripts. It changes in the same pull request as the code it describes. Exploratory scripts get no page; a script gets its page in the pull request that adds it to R/main.R.
Results pages exist only once outputs are cleared for release, either by the review AGENTS.md names or because setup decided they need none. A Results page reads the cleared files in tables/ and figures/. It never reruns the analysis or touches restricted data.
The four project-document pages show analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md. Those files stay at the top of the repository and are the only copies anyone edits; each page in quarto/ just displays its file when the site is built. The plan’s page uses GitHub-style section links, so the plan’s links to its own sections work both on GitHub and on the site. The Architecture page draws the diagrams in ARCHITECTURE.md, which would otherwise show as code, and shows a short note until that file exists. The other three files must exist before the site is first built, or the build stops.
What the assistant does with them. It writes and updates script pages, and adds a project-document page and sidebar entry when a new document at the top of the repository is to be shown on the site. For an existing site that lacks a Background or Study design page, it proposes an outline to the maintainer rather than adding a placeholder page, because that content belongs to the study team.

title: People on a project
text:
Written for version 0.1.14.
Projects outlast the people on them. Anyone can lead for a while and hand on, whether a student, resident, fellow or faculty member; clinicians and statisticians advise; the PI may decide, maintain the repository, or do the work. The plugin assumes none of these roles: it asks what you want to do and how much help you want. This section follows one person’s time on a project. Project stages follows the project itself.



Part
What happens

The rule that holds throughout: people decide and approve, and the assistant drafts and implements. Only the deciders named in the project’s AGENTS.md settle scientific questions.

title: Contributing in your role
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Sources: onboard-collaborator, onboarding, writing the analysis plan, the AGENTS.md template, GitHub workflow, review-analysis, blind reviewers.
The plugin assumes no role. It starts from what you want to contribute and what you already know, and offers the help that fits you. A project may have several people leading parts of it and no single lead, and the PI may use the plugin too. The roles below are common patterns, not boxes: one person can hold several, and each project fills them its own way.
Two rules hold in every role. Only a named decider settles a scientific question. And every change reaches the main branch through a pull request, a proposed change that others can see before it is merged.

Project lead
PI or maintainer
Decider
Clinician adviser

title: Leaving
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Sources: collaborator onboarding, onboard-collaborator skill, shared conventions, GitHub workflow, AGENTS.md template.
People leave projects all the time: a rotation ends, a job changes, someone hands their part to a colleague. The plugin’s aim is that the next person can carry on from the repository alone, without your files or your chats. So before your last session, the assistant works through four steps with you. Each step asks you; nothing is forced. Not everything can be finished, given an owner or closed, and a project may go dormant. What stays open is recorded, with the reason, rather than pushed onto someone.

title: Leaving
text:
How leaving starts
You. Tell the assistant you are leaving or handing over. Someone else can also ask for a handover from a person who is leaving. If you set up a check-in and gave it your end date, the check-in can raise it as that date approaches.
The assistant. It works through the steps below with you, before your last session. It asks at each step rather than deciding for you.
In the repository. Nothing yet.
Who decides. You choose what happens to each piece of your work. Scientific questions stay with the deciders named in the project’s AGENTS.md; leaving does not change who they are.
More. Join or leave a project; check-ins are described in On GitHub, not in files.

title: Leaving
section: Documents out of chats, laptops and email
text:
Documents out of chats, laptops and email
You. Think of anything that exists only in a chat, on your laptop or in your email: drafts, notes, data checks, and correspondence that settles something.
The assistant. It asks for these and offers to move each into the repository. It checks each against the project’s disclosure rules first. Anything holding results from restricted data that are not cleared for release stays where it is, and it tells you why. It shows you the exact text before posting anything as you.
In the repository. Each item becomes one of three things:

a draft pull request (a proposed change that is not yet ready to merge);
a comment on an existing issue;
a new issue.

Who decides. You choose what to move. The project’s disclosure rules decide what may not be moved.
More. The same habit applies at the end of every working session: see On GitHub, not in files.

title: Leaving
text:
Open issues and pull requests
You. Go through each open issue and pull request that is yours.
The assistant. For each one, it asks which of four things fits:

finish it;
hand it to someone;
close it with a reason;
leave it open with a note saying it is paused and what it is waiting on.

For an open pull request, it also writes down what remains, the order in which open pull requests should be merged, and any conflicts between them. It never merges a pull request itself.
In the repository. Notes on issues and pull requests, and some items closed with their reasons.
Who decides. You, with whoever takes an item on. A person, not an agent, merges a pull request. Closing an issue does not settle a scientific question; only a named decider does that.
More. Issues and pull requests; the plan and its decisions.

title: Leaving
text:
Requests with no answer yet
You. Think of what you have asked of others that has not been answered: an email to a collaborator, a question to the PI.
The assistant. It asks what these are and offers to record each one as an issue.
In the repository. One issue per request, saying who was asked, when, and what for. The question is then no longer held only in your inbox.
Who decides. You choose which to record.
More. Issues.

title: Leaving
text:
Ownership, last
You. This step applies only if you own the repository on GitHub.
The assistant. It raises transferring the repository to the PI. The plugin gives the steps as Settings → General → Transfer, and the new owner must accept within a day. The assistant cannot change GitHub settings; it tells the person who can.
In the repository. Issues, pull requests and history move with the repository, and old links to the repository redirect to the new address. The website does not: GitHub does not redirect it. After the transfer, someone must:

update the site and repository links in _quarto.yml (the website’s settings file), the site pages and the README;
re-render the site;
turn GitHub Pages on again under the new owner.

Who decides. The owner starts the transfer, and the new owner accepts it.
More. Transferring ownership and the website caveat; GitHub Pages; _quarto.yml; the README.

title: Leaving
PI or maintainer
Decider
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Part of Contributing in your role, which lists the sources.
You. Anyone AGENTS.md names for an area, such as a clinical question or the statistical methods. A project may have several deciders, each for their own area.
The assistant. It drafts each decision issue with the question, the options and the evidence, and asks you. A check-in can list each decision waiting on you, one line per option, with a link to the issue. It won’t choose for you, and it won’t say you decided something unless there is a written record of it.
In the repository. You state your choice in the decision issue. If you don’t use GitHub, you can decide by email or in a meeting. Whoever received your answer then posts your exact words in the issue, with your name, the date and how it was given. A summary or a memory of what you said doesn’t count. The decision takes effect when a pull request that rewrites the plan and closes the issue is merged.
Who decides. You, within your area. Anyone else may add options and evidence.
More. The plan and its decisions.

title: Join or leave a project

Leaving
When you say you are leaving, or a check-in sees your end date coming, the assistant works through four things with you:

Documents that exist only in a chat, on your laptop or in email, moved into the repository.

title: Start a project
text:
What it is for
Setting up a new analysis project, or tidying an existing one (a folder of scripts, or one long R Markdown file), so it becomes a GitHub repository in a consistent layout that the next person can pick up.

title: Start a project
text:
When to use it

You have an idea, a protocol or an old script, and no repository yet.
You have a repository that grew without a plan and want it organized.
A setup was started in an earlier chat and not finished.

title: Start a project
