title: Code and website
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Sources: AGENTS.md template, shared conventions, GitHub workflow, document-analysis skill, Quarto guidance, data sources.
Once the analysis plan says what to do, the work is writing R code that does it, and explaining that code on the project website. The two go together: a script that joins the analysis gets its web page in the same change. This page follows that stage from a first experiment to a published explanation.

title: Code and website
text:
Writing the code
You. You may explore freely. Experiments live on a branch (a separate working copy of the repository on GitHub) or a fork, need no web page, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when R/main.R runs it (in R terms, “sources” it). From then on, every rule in the project’s AGENTS.md applies to it. If you have access to restricted data, you are the one who runs the code on it; results on real data are produced by an authorised person, never by the assistant.
The assistant.

Writes R that a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides can read: pipes and dplyr verbs, case_when() instead of nested if, loops over names rather than clever shortcuts. Where base R is unavoidable, it goes in a named, tested function with a comment saying why.
Sends any code that touches a data source through that source’s package, as listed in the “Data sources” table of AGENTS.md. It reads the package’s documentation for the installed version first, rather than guessing from a function’s name.
Writes and tests the code on synthetic data: made-up data, built in code and labelled as such. It never reads restricted data, unless that table explicitly allows it for a source, and then only within those words.
Asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive calls.
Proposes, rather than commits, any other way of writing something already agreed, and shows whether the outputs stay identical.
Never makes a scientific choice in code. If the code would need to depart from the plan, it opens a decision issue (or comments on the existing one) for the deciders.
Never merges a pull request.

In the repository.

One branch per piece of work, and one pull request (a proposed change, shown on GitHub before it lands) to bring it into the main branch. Each pull request starts from the main branch.
A new definitive script gets its source() line in main.R and an update to ARCHITECTURE.md, in the same pull request.
Each pull request says which plan section or issue it addresses and what was checked. When the assistant opened it, it also says whether the checks were done by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
The checks come from the list in AGENTS.md: does the change follow the plan and leave open decisions open; does it use the data package as documented; does it name the package version relied on; do cohort steps, joins and reported numbers match the plan; is the structure current; does anything in the files, commit messages or pull-request text look like it came from restricted data; and does main.R run in a fresh session.
No results, counts or data values from restricted data go into any file, commit message, issue or pull request unless cleared for release.

Who decides. The plan’s named deciders make every scientific choice. Changing what the assistant may do with a data source is for a person, through a pull request that names the agreement permitting it; the assistant never proposes that change. How many approvals a pull request needs before merging is the team’s choice. Which tool you use for branches and pull requests is your own.
More. The code, Rules for working, On GitHub, not in files. For an independent check of code or a pull request, see Review.

title: Code and website
text:
Explaining the code
You. You read the page the assistant writes for each script, and check that it says what the code actually does. If you are a clinician, this page is written for you: it should make sense without reading R.
The assistant.

Gives each new definitive script its web page and its sidebar entry in the same pull request that adds it to main.R.
Divides the script into labelled sections, each starting with a comment line such as ## ---- step-name. Labels are unique across all scripts and never change what the code does.
Builds the page so it imports those sections from the script itself, with knitr::read_chunk(). The code on the page is therefore always the code that runs. The website never runs the analysis, so it is built without the analysis data.
Under each section, explains what the step does and why, what it takes in, which part of the plan it carries out, and what it hands on. It defines abbreviations, gives statistics their plain meaning, and does not describe associations as causes.
Cites sources from the project’s references.bib. It never invents a citation; a missing one is flagged for the librarian review.
Describes the code as it is. If code and plan disagree, the page says so rather than smoothing it over.
Keeps the Study design and methods page current. That page explains the study’s choices in plain language, with three kinds of note: Specified in (the plan section that defines a method), Current code (where the code does not yet do what the plan says, linked to the issue tracking it) and Decision pending.
Marks text that depends on an open decision. A paragraph starting with Decision pending: is highlighted in yellow and linked to its decision issue; the mark comes off when the decision is settled. Yellow is used for nothing else.
Refreshes ARCHITECTURE.md after a structural change: a script added, removed or reordered, or a change in how data flow between scripts.
Renders the site and looks at the changed pages, and reports static checks, a successful render and the visual check separately.
Does not change an existing site’s layout or wording without first listing the differences and asking.

In the repository.

A page in quarto/ named after the script, with its sidebar entry in _quarto.yml under Code, numbered in the order main.R runs it.
When code changes, the prose of every section whose behaviour changed is updated in the same pull request.
Publishing follows the route the project’s AGENTS.md records. Either the built site in docs/ is committed and served by GitHub Pages, or docs/ stays uncommitted and a GitHub Actions workflow builds and publishes it. The plugin does not yet provide that workflow.

Who decides. The project chooses its publishing route at setup. The site goes live only when someone with admin or maintainer permission on the repository turns on GitHub Pages; the assistant cannot change settings, so it tells that person the steps. What the site says about the science follows the plan and the deciders.
More. The website, The code (for ARCHITECTURE.md), Explain the code. For an independent check that pages match the code, see Review.

title: The plan
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Sources: writing the analysis plan, AGENTS.md template, shared conventions, GitHub workflow, blind reviewers, document-analysis skill, review-analysis skill.
The analysis plan, analysis-plan.md, says what the analysis must do. It is the project’s source of truth: the code carries out the plan and never redefines it. This page follows the plan through three stages: deciding what goes in it, locking it, and changing it after that. For how the file itself is laid out, see The plan and its decisions.

title: The plan
text:
Deciding the plan
You. Bring what the investigators already have: the protocol, the IRB approval, earlier scripts, papers. When the assistant lists the choices those materials already make, the deciders go through the list together and confirm or change each one. Anyone on the project can open a decision issue (a GitHub issue for one open scientific question) or add options, evidence and clinical reasoning to one.
The assistant.

Drafts the plan from the template that fits the study, and from the investigators’ materials.
Presents the choices the materials already make as one list, for the deciders to confirm or change.
Opens a decision issue for anything not confirmed, with the options and the evidence for each, and marks the open point in the plan with Open: and a link to the issue.
Checks codes and variable definitions against the data source’s own documentation for that release, rather than guessing from their names.
Cites every definition, threshold or method taken from a source with a key from the project’s references.bib. It never invents a citation or cites from memory.
Once a decider has stated a choice, it can write the plan change for it.
It won’t choose among the options, in the issue, the plan or the code. It won’t say someone decided something unless there is a written record of it.

In the repository.

analysis-plan.md at the top of the repository, with an Open: marker wherever a question is still open. On the project website, those paragraphs are highlighted in yellow.
One decision issue per open question. How they are marked (a label, a word in the title) is the project’s choice.
Entries in references.bib for every source the plan cites.
While the plan is a draft, git’s history is the record of changes: each design change is committed on its own, with the reason and whether any results that depend on it had already been seen.

Who decides. The deciders named in the project’s AGENTS.md, each in their own area. Only a decider settles a decision issue, by stating the choice in it.

A decider who doesn’t use GitHub can decide by email or in a meeting. Whoever received the decision posts the decider’s exact words in the issue, with their name, the date and how it was given. A summary or a memory of what was said doesn’t settle it.
A choice already settled in a signed protocol or IRB approval counts as decided, and is cited as such.
A decision takes effect when the plan changes. Once the decider has stated the choice, anyone may write the pull request that rewrites the passage, gives the reason, cites the evidence, removes the Open: marker and closes the issue. It counts when that pull request is merged into the protected default branch. An agent never merges it.

More. The plan and its decisions and References and README in the Manual; Start a project for the first draft and Explain the code for updating the plan after a decision.

title: The plan
text:
Locking the plan
You. Once the plan is final, lock it: before outcome data are analysed, or when the study is registered. Locking means that from then on every change is recorded openly, with its date and reason.
The assistant. When asked, it updates the plan for locking: it adds an empty section called “Amendments after locking”, and, if the study is registered, cites the registration and the tag in the plan’s header. Before that, a plan review can check that the plan is complete (see below). It won’t create the tag on its own.
In the repository.

The plan’s empty Amendments after locking section.
A tag on that commit, such as sap-v1.0. A tag is a fixed name for one saved version of the repository, so anyone can see exactly what the plan said when it was locked.
If the project uses milestones, “plan locked” can be one of them; the phases and dates are the team’s choice.

Who decides. The deciders decide that the plan is final. Tags are created by the maintainer, or with the maintainer’s explicit authorization.
More. The plan and its decisions and On GitHub, not in files in the Manual; Review for the Plan review, in which blind reviewers (a clinician reader, a clinician-researcher, a statistician and a librarian) check the plan against its reporting guideline, the question and its citations.

title: The plan
text:
Revisions after results
You. After locking, the plan can still change, but never silently. A change of scientific choice, including one a reviewer suggests, goes through a decision issue like any other choice.
The assistant.

Writes each agreed change as a dated entry in the Amendments after locking section: what changed, why, and whether it was made before or after outcome data were seen.
Treats a reviewer’s request to change the methods as a new scientific choice. It proposes a decision issue with the options and the reviewers’ arguments; the plan and code change only after a decider has settled it.
In a Plan ↔︎ code review, checks that every plan section has code and every analysis has a plan section, that each open point links an open decision issue, and that no open decision has been settled in the code.
It won’t make a quiet edit to a locked plan, and it won’t settle a decision issue.

In the repository.

A new dated entry under Amendments after locking for every change.
A new tag for each amended version, such as sap-v1.1.
The decision issue behind each amendment, closed by the pull request that made it.

Who decides. The named deciders, exactly as before locking. A reviewer, anyone on the project or an agent can raise the question and argue for an answer; only a decider settles it.
More. The plan and its decisions in the Manual; Review for acting on review findings; Explain the code for updating the plan and the website to match.

title: Results
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Sources: report skill, reporting guidance, review skill, blind reviewers, data handling, AGENTS.md template, Quarto guidance.
This page follows a project from its first tables to the moment its outputs can be made public. There are three stages: building the reporting, reviewing it, and clearing it for release. Throughout, the analysis plan decides what is reported, and restricted data never pass through the assistant.

title: Results
text:
Reporting
You. You ask the assistant to build the tables, figures and numbers the plan calls for. If you are the authorized person, you run the finished code on the real data in the approved environment. Before any output leaves that environment, you check it against the project’s disclosure rules.
The assistant. It works through a fixed order, using only the parts that fit the design:

Participant flow: the diagram of who was included and excluded (the STROBE flow diagram). It is built with the flowchart package by the same code that builds the analysis cohort, so the two cannot disagree.
Descriptions and missingness: every analysis variable, with its missing count shown, and the patterns of missing values.
Table 1, grouped the way the plan says, with gtsummary.
Two-variable and stratified summaries, where the plan calls for them.
Longitudinal structure, when the same people are measured repeatedly over time.
Time to event: follow-up, events and censoring, described before any model.
Figures, following the PSI/EFSPI graphics principles. Survival curves follow the KMunicate style: confidence intervals, and a table under the plot with the numbers at risk, censored and with events.
Model tables that report the model actually fitted.

What it won’t do:

It won’t choose the model, the covariates, how to handle missing data, or the target journal’s style. These come from the plan. Where the plan leaves one open, it opens or points to a decision issue (a GitHub issue for one open scientific question) instead.
It won’t read restricted data. It writes and tests the reporting code on synthetic data: made-up data built in code and labelled as synthetic. Real results come from an authorized person.

Small counts need care before anything leaves the approved environment. Every table, figure and flowchart box must pass the project’s disclosure rules, including counts someone could work out by subtraction. Numbers at risk shrink late in follow-up, so under a small-cell rule a survival curve ends, or its cells are hidden, before any count falls below the threshold. Figures that plot individual people are not published from restricted data. The threshold itself comes from each data source’s own agreement; the plugin does not set one.
Before finishing, the assistant checks that:

every count in tables, figures and text matches the flow diagram;
estimates, confidence intervals, model counts, reference groups and scales match the fitted model and are labelled correctly;
every number in the text comes from a computed value, never retyped;
every figure has a caption and alt text (a written description for readers who cannot see the image).

It says which checks ran on synthetic data and which were only read, and then offers an independent Reporting review.
In the repository. The reporting code, in R/tables.R and R/figures.R. These write their outputs to tables/ and figures/. Whether those folders are kept in Git depends on the project’s setup (see “Going public”).
Who decides. The plan decides what is reported and how. Open choices go to the deciders named in AGENTS.md. The assistant asks about the journal’s style rather than choosing one.
More. Report results; The code; The plan and its decisions; Rules for working.

title: Results
text:
Reviewing
You. You choose the kind of review, or describe what you want checked and let the assistant pick. After the review, you decide what happens to each finding.
The assistant. It offers several kinds of review:

Change: a pull request, a branch, or work not yet committed, checked against the plan and AGENTS.md.
Plan ↔︎ code, Plan, Site ↔︎ code and Architecture: whether the code, plan, website and ARCHITECTURE.md agree and are complete.
Repository conformance: whether the repository matches the blueprint.
Reporting: the flow diagram, tables, models and numbers in the text, checked against the cohort and what was fitted.
Release: covered under “Going public”.

A request for “a full review” runs the Plan, Plan ↔︎ code, Site ↔︎ code and Reporting reviews together.
A change review reads every file the change touches, not a sample. The report lists them, and names any file not read with the reason.
Most reviews use up to five blind reviewers: a clinician reader, a clinician-researcher, a statistician, a coding expert and a librarian. “Blind” means each one works on its own, as a separate agent where the host allows, and cannot see the other reviewers’ findings or the conversation that produced the work. Each gets a packet of the repository files its role reviews, and may also read public material its role needs: the data-access packages the analysis uses, the sources the work cites, and official code sets and reporting guidelines. No reviewer ever receives restricted data or outputs not yet cleared for release. Where the host cannot run independent agents, the report says that blindness was not guaranteed.
The assistant then combines the reports. Before it lists a finding as an error, it checks the claim against the source itself, and moves any claim that does not hold to a “Corrections” list. It merges duplicates, keeps disagreements visible without settling them, and numbers every finding.
What it won’t do: change anything during the review. Reviews are read-only. A finding that is really a scientific choice becomes a proposed decision issue; the assistant does not choose.
In the repository. Nothing, until you act. Then, finding by finding, you can keep the report, open GitHub issues, propose decision issues, post a pull-request review, fix chosen findings on a branch with a pull request, or ask for a re-review of what was fixed.
Who decides. You, the reader, decide what to act on, one finding at a time. Scientific choices still go to the named deciders.
More. Review; On GitHub, not in files.

title: Results
text:
Going public
You. Before the website, tables or figures go public, you ask for the Release review. A person signs off on its result.
The assistant. For the Release review it checks the files itself rather than using the blind reviewers. It checks that nothing from restricted data is included unless the review named in AGENTS.md has cleared it, that figures have alt text, and that no passwords or keys are included. It does not sign off; a person does.
In the repository.

At setup, the assistant asks whether the tables and figures need review before they can be public. If they don’t, tables/ and figures/ are tracked in Git from the start.
If they do, both folders stay out of Git (in .gitignore) until the review named in AGENTS.md clears them. Someone then removes the two lines from .gitignore and inspects the contents before adding them.
A Results page on the project website exists only for outputs cleared for release, by that review or because setup decided they need none. It reads the cleared files in tables/ and figures/, never reruns the analysis and never touches restricted data. It has the green Results look.
The published website never contains results from restricted data unless the named review has cleared them.

Who decides. The review named in AGENTS.md clears outputs for release, under the data agreement’s rules. A person signs off on the Release review. The assistant decides neither.
Submitting to a journal and publishing a paper are outside the plugin; it stops there.
More. Review; Rules for working; The website.

title: Getting started
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Sources: the initialize-analysis skill, the questionnaire, GitHub workflow, onboarding, shared conventions, data handling, personal instructions template, Quarto setup.
Every project starts somewhere: an idea, a protocol, an old R Markdown file or a folder of scripts. This page follows a project from that point until it has a repository, a draft plan, working rules and a starter website. The next person to join can then pick it up from the repository alone.

title: Getting started
text:
Before there’s a repository
You. You bring what exists: the idea, a protocol or IRB approval, earlier scripts, papers or a draft plan. If you have several versions of a script, you say which one is current; the assistant takes your word for it. You do not need R or Git to help at this stage. A clinician can work on the protocol from the browser.
The assistant.

It suggests creating the repository first, before drafting anything. Whoever is setting up can create it under their own account. Ownership can move later, for example when the person who set it up leaves.
If the repository has to wait (say, someone else will create it), it keeps drafts as files in your own assistant project for this repository, not only in the chat. It moves them into the repository once it exists.
It will not open files that may hold restricted data while it takes stock of your materials. Being able to see a file does not mean it may be published.

In the repository. Nothing yet. The drafts live in your assistant project until the repository exists.
Who decides. The person setting up decides where the repository is created and under whose account. Scientific choices are not made at this stage; they wait for the named deciders.
More. Start a project; On GitHub, not in files, which covers moving ownership when someone leaves.

title: Getting started
text:
Setting up
You. You answer a short questionnaire. The assistant asks one question at a time, and skips anything you have already told it or that is already in your files. The questions cover:

Deciders. Who makes the scientific decisions, and in which areas. If your protocol names investigators, the assistant suggests them for you to confirm or change. If no one is named yet, decision issues can be drafted but not settled until someone is.
Data boundaries. Which data the project uses, where they are kept and what agreement governs them. The assistant records the policy, never passwords or patient data.
Review before release. Whether the figures and tables need a review before they can be public. The assistant asks this directly rather than guessing from the data source.
Publishing route. Whether the website is built into a docs/ folder in the repository and served from there (the default), or built and published by a GitHub workflow instead.
Public or private. The plugin assumes a public repository on GitHub’s free plan. On that plan a private repository has neither a website (GitHub Pages) nor branch rulesets.
Layout. Whether an existing project keeps its own organisation or adopts the plugin’s blueprint, the intended layout.

The assistant. It turns your answers into a short setup plan, then drafts what you have agreed to:

The analysis plan (analysis-plan.md), from the template that fits the study. Each choice still open becomes a draft decision issue: a GitHub issue for one open scientific question. It does not pick an answer.
AGENTS.md, the shared rules for working here. It names the deciders and lists every data source with the package that reads it. For every restricted source, agents may do nothing beyond code, documentation and synthetic data, and the assistant does not suggest allowing more.
.gitignore, the list of files Git must never pick up. It is adapted from the starter, not copied blindly. Ignoring a file keeps it out of Git, but it does not stop an assistant from reading it.
A README, written as README.Rmd and knitted to README.md, unless you prefer a plain README.md.
The starter website, with all its pages, its stylesheet and the filter that highlights open decisions.

It also offers three things you can turn down:

Your own assistant project for this repository, with instructions filled in for how you like to work. It asks which working style you want to start from: review only, step by step, or hands-off.
Milestones: phases of the project with target dates, which your team chooses.
A periodic check-in that tells you what is waiting on you.

Finally it records the setup decisions, and anything still open, in one agreed setup note or an existing tracker, so a later chat can carry on without asking again. Your personal permissions stay in your own instructions, never in shared files.
What it will not do: choose a scientific option, install tools, publish anything, make changes on GitHub without your go-ahead, or change repository settings. If you set up from R, it suggests one command at a time based on what usethis::git_sitrep() shows; you run each one.
In the repository. At the root: analysis-plan.md, AGENTS.md, REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md (copied unchanged), .gitignore, the README, references.bib, the starter R/ scripts and the website files. ARCHITECTURE.md can come later, once there is code.
For an existing project, nothing that already exists is overwritten. The assistant compares each file with the starter and lists what differs. An existing website is brought up to date only after the maintainer agrees to that list. It is then done in one pull request, which keeps every page the site already has. Nothing is treated as disposable because it is old.
Who decides.

The maintainer, the person with admin rights on the repository, does two things in GitHub’s settings that the assistant only describes. First, protecting the main branch, so every change arrives through a pull request. Second, switching on GitHub Pages so the website goes live: once the first pull request containing docs/ is merged, or, with a workflow, once its first run has created the gh-pages branch.
The deciders settle every open scientific choice, in its decision issue.
You decide what the assistant may do for you, and whether to take up the optional offers.

title: Report results
text:
What it is for
Building the tables, figures and numbers a paper reports, so that every count and estimate comes from the code that produced it and matches the analysis plan.

title: Report results
text:
When to use it

You are ready to build the participant flow diagram, Table 1, survival curves or model tables.
You want to check that the numbers in a draft agree with each other and with what was fitted.

title: Report results
text:
What happens
The work follows a fixed order, using the parts that fit the design:

Participant flow: the diagram of who was included and excluded, built by the same code that builds the analysis dataset (with the flowchart package), so the two can’t disagree.
Descriptions and missingness: every analysis variable, with missing values shown.
Table 1, grouped the way the plan says (with gtsummary).
Two-variable and stratified summaries, where the plan calls for them.
Repeated measurements over time, where they exist.
Time to event: follow-up, events and censoring, before any model.
Figures, following the PSI/EFSPI graphics principles, with survival curves in the KMunicate style (numbers at risk, censored and with events under the plot) and rules for small counts.
Model tables that report the model actually fitted.

Before finishing it checks that every number reconciles with the flow diagram, that an analysis on fewer people than the cohort reports its own number, that proportional hazards were checked for any Cox model, that estimates and their labels match the fitted model, and that every number written in prose comes from a computed value, never retyped.
Not yet tested: the recipes for mixed models, GEE, overall p-values and multiple imputation have been checked against package documentation but not run.

title: Report results
text:
What it will not do

Choose the model, covariates or how missing data are handled. Those come from the plan; an open one becomes a decision issue.
Read restricted data. It writes and tests the code on made-up data; a person with access runs it on the real data, and every output passes the project’s disclosure rules before it leaves.

title: Review
text:
What it is for
Checking work before it is merged or made public: a single change, the plan, the website against the code, or the whole project.

title: Review
text:
When to use it

Before asking a colleague to look at a pull request.
When the plan is drafted, or before it is locked.
Before the website, tables or figures go public.
Whenever you want a second opinion on the project as it stands.

title: Review
text:
What happens
You choose the kind of review, or describe what you want checked and the assistant picks:







Review
What it checks




Change
A pull request or branch, every file it touches, against the plan and the project’s rules


Plan ↔︎ code
Every part of the plan has code, and the code settles nothing the plan leaves open


Plan
The plan is complete, its methods fit the question, and its citations say what it claims


Site ↔︎ code
The website explains the code as it is


Architecture
ARCHITECTURE.md matches the scripts


Repository
The required files, the data-sources table, .gitignore and protection of the main branch


Reporting
The flow diagram, tables, models and numbers in prose agree


Release
Nothing restricted or uncleared, no credentials, and alt text, before anything goes public; then a person signs off



Most reviews use some of five blind AI reviewers: a clinician reader, a clinician-researcher, a statistician, a coding expert and a librarian. Each works as a separate assistant with only the files its role needs and public material such as cited papers, without seeing the other reviewers’ findings or the conversation that produced the work. A final step checks every claimed error against the source before reporting it, and marks findings already known from issues. The AI reviewers don’t replace review by the team’s own clinicians and statistician.
With restricted data, reviewers see only the code and documentation, so a check that needs the data (model fit, for example) comes back as a focused check for a person with access to run.

text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Part of Contributing in your role, which lists the sources.
You. You move the analysis forward day to day: drafting the plan, writing code, opening pull requests, and keeping open questions moving. The lead can be anyone: a student, resident, fellow or faculty member. Several people may share this, and someone may take over from a lead who leaves.
The assistant.

If you know R but not GitHub, explains branches, commits and pull requests using the tool you already use. It doesn’t prescribe one.

In the repository. Your work arrives as pull requests that say which plan section or issue they address and what was checked. Before you leave, the assistant helps you move drafts, notes and unanswered requests out of your chats and laptop into issues or draft pull requests, and mark unfinished work as paused with what it is waiting on. The next person starts from the repository, not from your files.
Who decides. The deciders named in AGENTS.md. You decide too only if you are named there.

text:

You. You shape and check the design and analysis. You may be named in AGENTS.md as a decider for statistical areas, and you may review pull requests that change the analysis.
The assistant. It drafts options and evidence for statistical decision issues, and you or another named decider choose. You can ask it for a review of a change, the plan, or the plan against the code.
The review skill includes a statistician reviewer, but that is an AI agent, not you. It works blind: it sees only a packet of the plan, the methods and analysis pages, the analysis scripts and published tables, plus public material such as cited papers. It never sees restricted data, so a question that needs the data comes back as a focused check for an authorized person to run. Where the plan leaves a choice open, it comments on the options but doesn’t decide. Acting on its findings is your choice, finding by finding.
In the repository. Your choices in decision issues, your reviews on pull requests, and any issues opened from review findings you choose to act on.
Who decides. You, in the areas AGENTS.md assigns you. The AI reviewer never decides.

title: Joining
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Sources: onboard-collaborator skill, onboarding, personal instructions template, shared conventions, AGENTS.md template.
People join a project at any point: someone taking over from a lead who has left, a clinician asked for input, a statistician brought in for the methods. This page follows you through your first days, from finding where the project stands to setting up the help you want.

title: Joining
text:
Starting from the repository
You. You are new to the project, or you are taking over someone else’s work. You don’t need anything from the person before you.
The assistant.

It starts from the repository as it is now: the analysis plan, the open decision issues, the open pull requests and their notes, and anything the previous person left marked as paused.
It does not rely on the previous person’s files or chats.
It explains the project through its own documents and does not assume you can read code. The website is the way in for anyone who doesn’t code; a clinician starts at Clinical background and Study design and methods, and goes to the code pages only for detail.
Before asking you something, it looks for the answer in the repository and in earlier chats in your own assistant project, where it can see them. It asks only what is still unclear, and says what it found.

In the repository. These are the documents you will be shown:

analysis-plan.md, which says what the analysis must do. Its Open: markers point to questions still undecided.
GitHub issues, which hold those open decisions (decision issues) and known gaps between the code and the plan.
AGENTS.md, which says how work is done here, including the data rules and who the deciders are.
ARCHITECTURE.md, which says how the code fits together, for people who will work on it.

Who decides. Joining does not make you a decider. AGENTS.md names the deciders and their areas. Anyone may inform a decision with options, evidence or clinical reasoning; only a named decider settles it.
More. The plan and its decisions, Rules for working, Join or leave a project.

title: Joining
section: Help at the level you choose
text:
Help at the level you choose
You. Say what you want to contribute and what you already know. You can ask to learn as you go, or to have the assistant do more of the work with you.
The assistant.

It starts from your goal and gives one next step at a time, keeping your earlier answers.
For a clinician, it begins with the scientific question, the cohort, the outcomes and the protocol decisions still open.
For someone who knows R but not Git, it explains local files, commits, branches or forks, and pull request review, using the workflow you are actually allowed to use. (Git keeps the history of the files; a pull request is a proposed change that others review before it joins the main branch.)
It explains only the Git steps your own tool needs, and does not prescribe a tool. For deeper learning it points to Happy Git and GitHub for the useR.
It won’t require R, Git or Quarto for work that doesn’t need them.
It checks what is already installed and authorised before suggesting any installation. It treats the assistant’s connection to GitHub as separate from a working Git setup on your own computer.
It never asks you to paste a token or password. It won’t change account settings, install software or publish work without your say-so.

In the repository. Your contribution, in whatever form suits you:

Clinical input without code: a comment on a decision issue, a review of the plan or the site for clinical accuracy and clarity, or suggested literature.
Code: a change made on a branch and offered as a pull request, following AGENTS.md.
Review: anyone may ask for one through the review skill.

Who decides. You decide how much help you want and which tool you use. Joining does not change the data rules: restricted data stay with authorised people in approved environments, whatever your role.
More. On GitHub, not in files, Review.

title: Joining
text:
Your own assistant project
You. The assistant offers to help you create your own assistant project for this repository (the plugin calls it an LLM project), one per repository. It is an offer, not a requirement. Its instructions mean each chat starts with your context, so you don’t paste it each time.
The assistant. It fills in the plugin’s personal instructions template with you. It asks:

Which working style you want. Review only: it reads, reviews and suggests, and changes nothing. Step by step: it says what will change and waits for your yes. Hands-off: it builds agreed work on branches and opens pull requests without asking at each step. Without a style, it works step by step.
How you work with GitHub: through the assistant’s connection, from your own tools, or both.
Your role and the help you prefer, what it may do for you, your data access boundaries, and whether it may post anything as you without showing you first.

In every style, it shows you the exact text before posting or sending anything as you; hands-off covers only the pull requests it opens. Afterwards it walks you through what was made in your name. If it cannot edit your assistant’s settings itself, it gives you the text to paste and says so.
In the repository. Nothing. Your instructions live in your own assistant project and are not shared. The repository stays the shared record, so nothing others need should live only in your project.
Who decides. You choose your working style and may add stricter rules than AGENTS.md. Your instructions never loosen its rules on data, decisions or pull requests, and nothing in them can widen what agents may do with a data source.
More. Personal project instructions.

title: Joining
text:
The check-in
You. The assistant asks whether you want a periodic check-in, run as one of the assistant’s scheduled tasks where it has them. It is for anyone who asks, whatever their role. You choose how often it runs.
The assistant. The check-in always reports what is waiting on you:

issues assigned to you;
decisions you make, each with the question, each option in a line, and a link to the decision issue;
pull requests awaiting your review.

You can also choose to include what you are waiting on from others, work with no recent activity, and milestones due soon. It can look over your recent chats in your own assistant project for drafts that never reached the repository, and offer to save them. If you have email connected and want it, it reviews only your messages about this project and proposes where to record each decision or request. Anything holding results from restricted data not cleared for release stays where it is, and you are told why.
What it won’t do: it reads the repository and may draft messages, but it never posts or sends anything on its own.
In the repository. Nothing changes unless you agree to save something there. Your check-in and email choices are recorded in your own instructions, not in shared files.
Who decides. If you are a decider, you can decide from the check-in, but the decision itself is recorded in the decision issue.
More. The setup note and check-ins, Join or leave a project.

You. You bring clinical knowledge. You don’t need R, Git or Quarto, and the assistant won’t ask you to learn them for work that doesn’t need them.

title: References and README
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Source: starter references.bib, guideline entries, writing the analysis plan, shared conventions, starter README.Rmd, document-analysis skill, initialize-analysis skill, repository blueprint.
Three things in a project hold its evidence and introduce it to visitors: the bibliography file references.bib, the references/ folder of supporting documents, and the README that GitHub shows on the repository’s front page. This page explains what each one holds and how the assistant treats it.

title: References and README
text:
references.bib
What it is. The project’s bibliography: one entry for each paper, guideline or data guide the project cites. It is a BibTeX file, a plain-text format that lists each source’s authors, title, journal, year and identifiers under a short key such as vonelm2007strobe.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository. The website’s settings (_quarto.yml) point to it, so the plan and the site pages draw their reference lists from this one file.
What’s in it. Only verified entries. Each one must resolve to a real source through a DOI, a PubMed ID (PMID), or an official web address together with the release or version used. A new project starts with an empty file that holds only a comment: the plugin adds no example citations.
How it is used. Every definition, threshold, code list, parameter value or method taken from an outside source cites its entry with [@key]. For example, a sentence in the plan might end “… following the STROBE statement [@vonelm2007strobe].” The plan’s References section is built from this file; nobody types a reference list by hand. For data documentation, such as a data provider’s researcher guide or data dictionary, the citation names the specific release and the appendix, section or page.
Reporting-guideline entries. The plugin carries a separate file of verified entries for the reporting guidelines its plan templates name (STROBE, RECORD, CHEERS 2022, TARGET and TRIPOD+AI), with metadata checked against PubMed. It is a supply to copy from, not part of the project. Copy into the project’s references.bib only the entries its plan actually cites.
What it never holds. An invented citation, or one written from memory without checking the entry.
What the assistant does with it. It cites from this file in the plan and on the site pages, using [@key] rather than bare links. When a statement needs a source that isn’t in the file, it flags the gap for the librarian reviewer rather than guessing. The librarian reviewer checks that every entry resolves and has the right metadata, that every key used is in the file, and that each citation supports the sentence it is attached to. It proposes new entries; the person reading the review decides which to add.

title: References and README
text:
The references/ folder
What it is. A folder of supporting technical detail and evidence. It backs up the plan; it is not a second analysis plan.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository, next to references.bib.
What’s in it. What each project needs, which differs from project to project. Typical documents:

data dictionaries and release notes from a data provider;
operational definitions and code lists;
evidence summaries and notes on an API (a service that code queries for data);
worked examples on synthetic data that have been checked.

Facts about a data source that the project relies on, when the source’s package is maintained by someone else, also go here, with a citation to the provider’s documentation (or in the plan, when they shape a decision).
How documents are kept. Markdown (.md) is preferred for text people consult often. Each document keeps its provenance: where it came from, the version or release, the source address, and the page or section. A converted copy is labelled as derived, and the original is kept as well when its formatting matters. The folder holds no empty placeholder files.
What it never holds. Private IRB materials, restricted data, or copies of papers the project has no licence to publish. Being given a file for review is not permission to publish it, and a public repository publishes everything in it.
What the assistant does with it. When setting up a project, it suggests documents that would be useful here, in Markdown, and helps add them. Having access to a file doesn’t mean it may be published, so it keeps the limits above.

title: References and README
text:
README.Rmd and README.md
What it is. The README is the repository’s overview: GitHub shows README.md on the repository’s front page. It tells a visitor what the project is, where the website is, and how to run the code.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository. README.Rmd is optional. When it exists, it is the source: people edit the .Rmd and re-knit it, which regenerates README.md. When there is no .Rmd, people edit README.md directly. Which of the two a project uses is the project’s choice, recorded in its AGENTS.md.
What’s in it. The starter README.Rmd has five parts:







Part
What it says




Badges
Small labels at the top giving the project’s status. The starter’s say “preliminary analysis”, “methods under development” and “not for citation”; a licence badge is included but switched off.


Goal
One sentence on the question, and the data sources used. It also says the analysis is in progress.


Website link
The address of the project website, which explains the code step by step.


Documentation
Links to analysis-plan.md (what the analysis is meant to do), ARCHITECTURE.md (how the code is organised), AGENTS.md (how to work in the repository) and the GitHub issues (open decisions and known gaps).


How to run
Run R/main.R from the project root, and name any restricted data and the package that locates it.



What it never holds. Results, until the figures and tables are cleared for public release. The starter leaves a note marking where they would go.
Who edits it. Anyone, through a pull request, like any other file.
What the assistant does with it. When setting up a project, it creates README.Rmd from the starter and knits README.md, unless the person prefers a plain README.md. After that, where there is a README.Rmd, it edits only that file. It keeps the status badges accurate, so a badge that says “preliminary” is changed when that stops being true. If the repository moves to a new owner, the website and repository links in the README are among those to update.

text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Part of The website, which lists the sources.
What it is. The built site is written to docs/. There are two ways to put it online, and each project chooses one. Its AGENTS.md records which, in the “Quarto website” section.








Route
docs/ in the repository?
Who builds the site




docs/ committed
Yes, committed with each change
The person making the change, before opening the pull request


Published by a workflow
No; listed in .gitignore
A GitHub Actions workflow (an automated job on GitHub), on every push to the default branch



On the first route, the site is rebuilt on the same branch as the change it reflects, and the rebuilt docs/ goes in the same pull request.
On the second route, the workflow file lives in .github/workflows/. The plugin doesn’t provide one yet. Each person still builds the site on their own computer before opening a pull request, to check it.
Turning it on. The site goes live only after someone with admin or maintainer permission turns on GitHub Pages in the repository’s Settings → Pages. Under “Build and deployment”, Source is set to Deploy from a branch; then the default branch and the /docs folder are chosen for the first route, or the gh-pages branch (which the workflow creates on its first run) and the / (root) folder for the second. A maintainer who works in R can do the first route with usethis::use_github_pages(). On GitHub’s free plan, a private repository can’t use Pages.
What the assistant does. It never changes repository settings. It tells the person who can, and gives them these steps.

title: Styles, 404 and extensions
text: Written for version 0.1.14. Part of The website, which lists the sources.

title: Styles, 404 and extensions
text:
styles.css and quarto/_pending.lua
What they are. Two small files that add the site’s visual cues: the coloured sidebar icons, and the yellow marks on provisional text.
What’s in styles.css. The colour for each sidebar icon, tied to the icon itself rather than to a position in the sidebar, so pages can be added or moved without editing it. It also makes section headings bold, adds a thin rule between sections, makes the sections under Code a little lighter, and sets the yellow used for provisional text. A project that already has a styles.css keeps its own rules and adds these.
What _pending.lua does. It is the filter that adds the yellow marks while the site is built. It highlights:

any paragraph that starts with Decision pending:;
on the analysis plan’s page only, any paragraph that contains the plan’s Open: marker;
any phrase written as [text]{.pending}, wherever it is, table cells included.

A page with at least one mark also gets a yellow ⏳ box at the top, headed “Provisional”, that says highlighted text depends on a decision the plan has not yet made.
The filter marks whole paragraphs only. A Decision pending: note inside a bullet or a table cell isn’t marked, so it is written as its own paragraph or wrapped as [text]{.pending}.
What it never does. Yellow means “an open decision could change this” and nothing else. A mark is removed when its decision is settled.

title: Styles, 404 and extensions
text:
404.qmd
What it is. The page GitHub Pages shows when someone follows a link to an address that doesn’t exist. Quarto doesn’t make one on its own.
What’s in it. A short note that the page isn’t on the site, a link to the home page, and a pointer to the search box. It is built from the top of the repository, so its links work from any address once the site’s address is set in _quarto.yml. It has no sidebar entry.

title: Styles, 404 and extensions
text:
_extensions/
What it is. The folder where Quarto keeps add-ons the site uses. It is committed with the repository.
What’s in it.

custom-callout (required). The MIT-licensed coatless-quarto/custom-callout extension turns the three callouts defined in _quarto.yml into the coloured boxes. Its code isn’t bundled in the plugin. It is added with quarto add coatless-quarto/custom-callout, or copied from another repository that has it, and the assistant installs it only when authorised.
Reader comments (optional). The issue-comments extension lets a reader highlight text and leave a comment, which is filed as a GitHub issue in the repository. It needs a relay and a GitHub App set up once, then three things switched on together for each site: the extension in _extensions/, the filter line in _quarto.yml, and the issue-comments: settings block. With all three on, the yellow Pending box also tells readers how to comment. Whether to use it is the project’s choice.

title: The plan and its decisions
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Source: writing the analysis plan.
Two things decide the science of a project: one file, analysis-plan.md, and the decision issues on GitHub that hold the questions it hasn’t settled yet. This page explains both, and how a question moves from one to the other.

title: The plan and its decisions
text:
analysis-plan.md
What it is. The plan says what the analysis must do: the question, the population, the definitions, the outcomes, the statistical methods and the sensitivity analyses. It is the project’s source of truth. The code carries out the plan and never redefines it; if the two disagree, the plan wins until a decider changes it.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository, as an ordinary Markdown file. The project website shows it on its Analysis plan page, read from this one file, so there is never a second copy to keep up to date.
What’s in it. The assistant drafts it from a template that fits the study:







Study
Reporting guideline it follows




Observational, using routinely collected data (registries, claims, health records)
STROBE and RECORD


An observational study with a causal question
the same, and TARGET if the design emulates a target trial


Economic evaluation or decision model
CHEERS 2022


Descriptive, geographic or access analysis
STROBE and RECORD, framed as descriptive



Every plan ends with the same sections: disclosure control (the data agreement and its small-cell rule), limitations, a reporting map that links each checklist item to the section that answers it, and the references.
What it never holds. Results, notes on how far the code has got, how the scripts are organised, or working rules. Those belong in the outputs, in GitHub issues, in ARCHITECTURE.md and in AGENTS.md.
Who edits it. Anyone can propose a change, through a pull request. A change to a scientific choice counts only once a named decider has made that choice.
What the assistant does with it. It drafts the plan from the investigators’ protocol, IRB approval, earlier scripts and papers, and lists the choices those materials already make, for the deciders to confirm. It checks codes and variable definitions against the data source’s own documentation rather than guessing from their names. Every definition or threshold taken from a paper or a data guide is cited from the project’s references.bib; it never cites from memory.
What you see on GitHub. A readable document. Points still open are marked like this:

The exposure cut-off. Open: #14

On the project website, a paragraph like that is highlighted in yellow.

title: The plan and its decisions
text:
Decision issues
What they are. A decision issue is a GitHub issue for one open scientific question. It states the question, the options and the evidence for each. Projects mark them however they like (a label, a word in the title); the plugin doesn’t prescribe one.
Who takes part. Anyone can open one or add to it: options, evidence, clinical reasoning, a paper. Only a decider settles it. The project’s AGENTS.md names the deciders and their areas, for example “statistical methods: the study statistician”.
Deciding without GitHub. A decider can answer by email or in a meeting. Whoever received the answer posts the decider’s exact words in the issue, with their name, the date and how it was given. A summary or a memory of what was said doesn’t settle it.
What the assistant does. It drafts the options and the evidence, and asks the deciders. It never chooses, in the issue, the plan or the code, and it never says someone decided something unless there is a written record of it.

title: The plan and its decisions
text:
From open question to decision

Someone notices a choice the plan hasn’t made, and opens a decision issue.
People add options and evidence.
The named decider states the choice in the issue, or someone posts their emailed words there.
A pull request rewrites that passage of the plan to state the decision and its reason, cites the evidence, removes the Open: marker, and closes the issue.
The decision takes effect when that pull request is merged into the main branch. The code can then follow the plan.

title: The plan and its decisions
text:
Locking the plan
What it means. Once the plan is final, and before anyone looks at outcome data, it is locked: an empty “Amendments after locking” section is added, and that version is tagged (for example sap-v1.0). If the study is registered, the plan’s header cites the registration.
After locking. Every change gets a dated entry in that section: what changed, why, and whether it was made before or after outcome data were seen. Each change gets a new tag (sap-v1.1, and so on). A reviewer who asks for a new analysis therefore produces an amendment, decided like any other question, not a quiet edit.
Before locking, git’s history is the record: each design change is committed on its own, with the reason and whether any dependent results had already been seen.

title: _quarto.yml and the home pages
text: Written for version 0.1.14. Part of The website, which lists the sources.

title: _quarto.yml and the home pages
text:
_quarto.yml
What it is. The settings file for the whole site: its title, its look, its sidebar and which pages it builds.
Where it lives. At the top of the repository, next to index.qmd, 404.qmd and styles.css. The explanatory pages sit in the quarto/ folder.
What’s in it.

Site settings. The site’s address, the repository’s address and its default branch (the repository’s actual main branch, whatever it is called) are filled in before the site is first built. A render: list names the pages to build (index.qmd, 404.qmd and everything in quarto/), so the Markdown documents at the top of the repository don’t also turn into stray pages.
The look. The cosmo theme with styles.css, a table of contents on each page, and code folded away behind a “Click to show/hide R Code” button.
The sidebar. Docked on the left, with search, and every section starts open. Each entry points to a page’s source file and only to pages that exist. Each entry also carries an icon for its kind of page (see the table below).
Callouts. A callout is a coloured box on a page. Three are defined here: a pink Rcode box (💻), a green Results box (📊) and a yellow Pending box (⏳).
Filters. Small programs that adjust each page as it is built. The starter runs quarto/_pending.lua first, then custom-callout. A third, for reader comments, is present but switched off.
The rule that nothing runs. One setting stops every chunk of code on the site from running:
execute:
  eval: false
Only a few chunks may switch this back on: the hidden import that reads a script’s code, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md as text, site helpers that read code or text and never data, and Results pages that read outputs already cleared for release. The project’s AGENTS.md lists any others it allows.

Who edits it. Whoever adds or moves a page, through a pull request. A new script’s sidebar entry goes in the same pull request as the script.
What the assistant does with it. It fills in the starter’s placeholders, adds a sidebar entry with the right icon for each new page, and numbers code pages in the order R/main.R runs them. On a site built before these conventions, it lists how the site differs and changes nothing until the maintainer agrees.

title: _quarto.yml and the home pages
text:
index.qmd and quarto/about.qmd
What they are. The Home page and the About page, the two pages a new reader is most likely to open first.
What’s in them.

Home (index.qmd, sidebar icon house): a brief clinical background, what the analysis does, a short methods summary that points to Study design and methods and to the analysis plan, and the project’s status (preliminary, under review or final), with links to the open decision issues.
About (quarto/about.qmd, sidebar icon info-circle): the study and who makes its scientific decisions; how the repository is organised and where the data live; how the site was made, including any AI assistants and the limits they work under; the four project documents, each in one line; and a one-line description of every page in the sidebar.

About is the only page that ends with a list of the other pages. Elsewhere the sidebar already does that job.
Who edits them. The study team, through pull requests. When a script gets a page, its line on About is added in the same pull request.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
Written for version 0.1.14. Full procedure: testing/README.md, Test B. Scenario: scenario.md.
Every person in this test, and in its records, is a simulated persona played by an AI agent. None of them is a real person, and the project uses only public data.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
What it tests
Whether a person with no GitHub account and no R can start a project from nothing with the plugin, and whether the people who come after can pick it up from the repository alone, through to a finished, reviewed analysis.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
The project
A new observational analysis: is an elevated level of serum free light chains associated with death from any cause, independent of age, sex and kidney function? It uses the public flchain dataset from the R survival package, which needs no data agreement.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
The panel



Persona
Who they are
File




Student lead 1
A medical student on a four-week elective; never used GitHub; no R on her laptop
student-novice.md


Student lead 2
An MD/MPH student who knows R but not Git; arrives with no handover
student-r-no-github.md

A busy physician-investigator who maintains the repository; terse, skims, uses only GitHub’s website and email

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
The roles in a run

Assistant: stands in for ChatGPT with the plugin installed. A fresh one for every session, because a new chat remembers nothing. It follows only the plugin. Its brief: assistant-brief.md.
Personas: one per person, kept across that person’s sessions, because people remember even when chats don’t. A persona never sees the plugin and writes only what the person would type.
Check-in: stands in for a scheduled task, run fresh each time it is due, reporting what is waiting on its person.
Orchestrator: passes messages word for word, carries out website actions a person says they did (creating a repository, merging, switching on the site), injects the scenario’s events, keeps the gap log, and never helps either side.

The world they share, a simulated GitHub made of folders, issues and pull requests as files, and email inboxes, is described in world.md.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
The scenario
Fourteen steps take the project from the first student’s first hour to a resubmitted paper: a first pull request, the PI’s review, input from the clinician by email and the statistician on GitHub, decisions, the first student leaving without being prompted to hand over, a second student arriving with nothing but the repository link, the statistician pushing to change the model, a blind review of the finished repository, the PI finishing the analysis, and a revision lead handling reviewer comments six months later.
A variant has the first student create the repository under her own account, to test whether anything raises transferring it before she leaves, and whether the website survives the transfer.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
How it is scored
For each person: how many exchanges before a first real contribution; whether they understood what was built in their name; jargon left unexplained; anything the assistant got wrong about the repository; any time it asked for installs, tokens or data it shouldn’t have; and any decision it made that belonged to a decider. Then a list of checks on the plugin’s own rules, each with the exchange that shows it. For the handover: how long the next lead took to find out where things stood, and what they could not recover.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
Rules for the orchestrator
Each comes from an error in an earlier run: relay by copying from the saved file, never by summary; personas write their own text; compute every number given to anyone; never supply invented content from a real publication; label simulated state; give no hints to either side; keep each person’s workspace separate; and run each check-in when it is due rather than assuming its output.
Results are on Runs.

title: Blind review (Test A)
text: Written for version 0.1.14. Full procedure: testing/README.md, Test A. Reviewer prompts: reviewers.md.

title: Blind review (Test A)
text:
What it tests
The plugin’s review uses five reviewers, each a separate assistant:

Clinician reader: is it clear, relevant and understandable to a clinician?
Clinician-researcher: are the definitions, cohort and outcomes clinically valid?
Statistician: do the methods fit the question, and does the code do what the plan says?
Coding expert: is the code correct, readable, and safe to keep in a public repository?
Librarian: do the citations exist, and do they say what the plan claims they say?

Test A checks whether these reviewers find real problems, keep to their roles, and never step outside the data rules.

title: Blind review (Test A)
text:
How it runs

Pick a public repository and fix one commit. Every reviewer reads the same version.
Build one packet per reviewer: only the files that reviewer’s role reviews, copied from that commit.
Start each reviewer as a separate assistant with a fresh context. It sees its packet and public material its role needs (package documentation, cited papers, code sets, guidelines), and never the other reviewers’ reports or the conversation that produced the work.
Combine the reports. Every claimed error is checked against the source before it is listed; anything that doesn’t hold is withdrawn or downgraded and listed under corrections. Findings already known from the repository’s issues are marked with their status.
Score each reviewer: did it stay in its role; how many findings were verified, withdrawn or unverifiable; which findings no other reviewer made; where reviewers independently found the same thing; what it said it couldn’t assess and why; and any breach of the data rules (there should be none).

title: Blind review (Test A)
section: What a good result looks like
text:
What a good result looks like
Reviewers that each find something the others missed, independent rediscovery of the same problem by more than one, few withdrawn claims, and no data-rule breaches. A reviewer that says it couldn’t check something points either to a fault in how its packet was built, which is then fixed, or to a real limit.
Results are on Runs.

title: R Analysis Workflow
text:
Written for version 0.1.14.
An early version. It has been tested in simulated projects and used by the maintainer on his own analyses; it has not yet been used by other teams.

title: R Analysis Workflow
text:
What it is
R Analysis Workflow is a plugin for ChatGPT and Claude. A plugin is a set of instructions the assistant reads when a task calls for them, so it works the same way every time and in every chat. This one is for biomedical analyses written in R, whose code and methods are published on GitHub and explained on a website. It is not for building R packages.
With the plugin installed, you ask in plain words (“Help me start this project”, “I’m joining this project and I’m new to GitHub”) and the assistant follows the plugin’s steps.

title: R Analysis Workflow
R Analysis Workflow
section: What a project built with it has
text:
What a project built with it has

An analysis plan (analysis-plan.md) that decides the science. The code does what the plan says.
Decision issues on GitHub for each scientific question still open. Only the named deciders settle them; the assistant drafts the options and never chooses.
R code in labelled sections, with the analysis run from one script.
A website that explains each step of the code in plain language for a clinician reader. It shows the real code, and never runs the analysis.
AGENTS.md, the rules any assistant follows in that project: who decides what, which data it may never read, and how changes are made.
Pull requests for every change to the main branch, so each change can be seen and checked before it goes in.
Locking the plan: once the plan is final, it is frozen before results are seen; any later change is recorded as a dated amendment.

title: R Analysis Workflow
text:
Where to start

New here? Read Start here.
Install the plugin.
Then, depending on what you are doing: start a project, join or leave one, explain the code, report results or review the work.
To see how the plugin is checked, read How it’s tested and Problems it solves.

title: R Analysis Workflow
text:
Before you rely on it
The plugin guides an assistant; it does not check your science. Review what the assistant produces as you would a new collaborator’s work, before it goes into a plan, a paper or a decision. VALIDATION.md lists what has and has not been tested.
The source, including every instruction the assistant reads, is on GitHub. Original text and code are MIT licensed.
